a: Judaism
p: The Greek noun for "Judaism" first appears in 2 Maccabees, set against "Hellenism".
b: The noun Ioudaismos is first found in 2 Maccabees (2:21; 8:1; 14:38). It was formed like Hellēnismos, "Hellenism", the Greek way of life that Jason brought into Jerusalem (4:13). For this writer, Judaism is not only a faith but a whole way of living under the law, which some held on to while others gave it up. Paul uses the same word for his own life before he followed Christ (Galatians 1:13–14), and that is its only use in the New Testament.
orig: ἐν τῷ Ἰουδαισμῷ (en tō Ioudaismō), 'in Judaism'

a: to hear the blood that was crying out to him
p: The prayer recalls Abel's blood crying to God from the ground.
b: The image comes from the first murder: "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Here the blood is that of the martyrs and of the people killed in Jerusalem (5:11–14; 6:10–11; 7). The prayer asks God to do what the youngest brother asked just before he died, to let his anger against the nation come to an end (7:37–38). Revelation 6:9–10 gives the same cry to the souls under the altar.

a: the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy
t: The turning point of the book
p: The martyrs' deaths end the time of wrath; from here on God fights for the Jews.
b: The writer has explained that the persecution was discipline for the people's sins (6:12–16), and the youngest brother prayed that his death and his brothers' would stop the Almighty's anger (7:37–38). Now that anger "turns to mercy", and Judas becomes unbeatable. Van Henten and others take the verse to mean that the martyrs' suffering counted for the nation; others say only that the time of punishment had run out. Whether one person's suffering can help others is the question of the card on 7:37–38.

a: Philip
p: This is probably Philip the Phrygian, the governor Antiochus left in Jerusalem (5:22).
b: Two men named Philip appear in these chapters. The one here is most likely the Phrygian whom Antiochus left as governor of Jerusalem, "with ways more savage than the one who placed him there" (5:22), and who reported Jews keeping the Sabbath in caves (6:11). The Philip of 9:29, the king's companion from childhood, is a different man: the one 1 Maccabees says Antiochus named as regent on his deathbed (1 Maccabees 6:14–15).

a: He chose Nicanor son of Patroclus
p: 1 Maccabees has Lysias send three generals with 47,000 men; here Ptolemy sends Nicanor with 20,000.
b: The two books tell this campaign differently. In 1 Maccabees, Lysias, regent while the king was in the east, sends three generals, "Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, Nicanor and Gorgias", with "forty thousand men and seven thousand horsemen" (1 Maccabees 3:38–39). Here Philip writes to Ptolemy, the governor of the province, and Ptolemy sends Nicanor with twenty thousand and Gorgias as his second. 1 Maccabees makes Gorgias the leader of the night attack and the real enemy (1 Maccabees 4:1–5); this book makes Nicanor the villain, perhaps to prepare for the Nicanor of chapters 14–15, whose defeat ends the book; whether he is the same man is uncertain.

a: what the king owed the Romans in tribute, two thousand talents
p: The Seleucids owed Rome a huge war payment from the peace of Apamea in 188 BC.
b: After Rome defeated Antiochus III, the peace of Apamea (188 BC) made him pay twelve thousand talents in yearly installments over twelve years (Polybius 21.42). Livy reports that an envoy of Antiochus IV brought overdue payments to Rome in 173 BC (Livy 42.6). Whether any debt was still owed in 165 BC is doubtful, and the "two thousand talents" may be the writer's estimate. The picture of the Jews being sold to pay Rome fits the book's view that the Seleucid kings were themselves under a greater power.

a: offering ninety slaves for one talent
p: A talent was six thousand drachmas, so Nicanor offered each Jew for about sixty-seven drachmas.
b: Nicanor planned to pay his debt in people. At ninety to the talent, each captive would go for less than seventy drachmas, a low price for a slave in this period, meant to bring buyers quickly. 1 Maccabees tells of the same merchants: they "came to the camp to buy the Israelites as slaves" (1 Maccabees 3:41). The writer adds his own comment: the man who sold others before he caught them (8:14) would himself flee "like a runaway slave" (8:35).

a: Then the cowards, who had no faith in God's justice, slipped away
p: The law of war sends the fainthearted home; here they simply desert.
b: Deuteronomy's law of war says: "Is anyone afraid and fainthearted? Let him go back home, so that his brothers' hearts do not melt like his" (Deuteronomy 20:8; compare Judges 7:3). 1 Maccabees has Judas apply that law with care: he sends home "those who were building houses, or were engaged to be married, or were planting vineyards, or were afraid... as the law says" (1 Maccabees 3:56). 2 Maccabees tells it as a judgment on the deserters: they "had no faith in God's justice".

a: his holy and majestic name had been called over them
p: To have God's name called over a people means they belong to him.
b: The phrase comes from the covenant blessing: "Every people on earth will see that the LORD's name has been called over you, and they will stand in fear of you" (Deuteronomy 28:10). It is used of the Temple and the city as well (Jeremiah 7:10; Daniel 9:19). The men ask to be saved "if not because of who they were": not for their own merit, but for the covenant with their ancestors and for the honor of God's name.

a: "Those men rely on their weapons and their daring," he said, "but our trust is in God Almighty.
p: Judas's words take up an old contrast between trusting in weapons and trusting in God.
b: The contrast is an old one in Israel's prayers and speeches. Hezekiah told his people before Sennacherib's attack: "He has an arm of flesh. We have the LORD our God, to help us and fight our battles for us" (2 Chronicles 32:8). The psalm says, "These have chariots, and those have horses, / but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7). Judas next names Sennacherib himself (8:19). "With one nod" uses a Greek word for a god's nod of command.

a: the help in Sennacherib's day, when a hundred and eighty-five thousand were destroyed
p: Judas recalls the Assyrian army struck down outside Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day.
b: Kings tells it this way: "The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria: one hundred eighty-five thousand" (2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36). 2 Maccabees returns to the story in Judas's last prayer before the final battle, where he asks God to send "a good angel" as he did then (15:22–23), and 1 Maccabees has Judas recall it too (1 Maccabees 7:41). For these writers it was the model of a rescue of Jerusalem by heaven alone.

a: the battle against the Galatians in Babylonia
t: A battle no one else records
p: No other source mentions this battle, though Jews did serve as soldiers for the Seleucid kings.
b: The Galatians were Celts who had crossed into Asia Minor in the 270s BC and fought as raiders and hired troops across the region. No other source tells of Jewish soldiers beating them in Babylonia, and scholars guess at a date in the wars of the 200s BC. Jewish troops in royal service are well attested. Josephus quotes a letter of Antiochus III moving "two thousand families of Jews" from Mesopotamia and Babylon to garrison places in Asia Minor, because he trusted them (Antiquities 12.149–150). On the numbers in this verse, see the variant.

a: Simon, Joseph and Jonathan
p: Judas's brothers in 1 Maccabees are John, Simon, Eleazar and Jonathan; there is no Joseph.
b: 1 Maccabees names the five sons of Mattathias: John called Gaddi, Simon, Judas, Eleazar called Avaran, and Jonathan called Apphus (1 Maccabees 2:2–5). This verse has Joseph instead of John, and 10:19 has a Joseph again beside Simon. Either the writer's source used another name, or "Joseph" is an old error for "John". 1 Maccabees 5:18 and 5:56 name a commander Joseph son of Zechariah, who was not one of the brothers.

a: he read aloud from the holy book
p: Before the battle Judas reads from "the holy book", as the law of war asked a priest to speak to the army.
b: Deuteronomy tells a priest to come forward before battle and say, "Do not let your hearts grow faint" (Deuteronomy 20:2–4). 1 Maccabees tells of the same moment differently: at Mizpah "they spread out the scroll of the law" (1 Maccabees 3:48). "The holy book" here is probably the law of Moses, perhaps the passage in Deuteronomy itself. The watchword "God's help" echoes the name Eleazar, which means "God has helped" in Hebrew. On who did the reading, see the variant.

a: they slaughtered over nine thousand of the enemy
p: 1 Maccabees counts three thousand enemy dead at Emmaus, against nine thousand here.
b: 1 Maccabees says that in this battle near Emmaus "about three thousand of them fell" (1 Maccabees 4:15), and that Judas had only three thousand men, short of shields and swords (1 Maccabees 4:6). Here Judas has six thousand (8:16), and over nine thousand enemy fall. Josephus follows 1 Maccabees. Large and round numbers are common in ancient war stories; 2 Maccabees uses them freely (10:17, 23, 31; 11:11), and historians trust neither book's figures.

a: for it was the day before the Sabbath, and for that reason they did not keep up the chase
t: Stopping the pursuit for the Sabbath
p: Judas breaks off a winning chase to keep the Sabbath, a detail 1 Maccabees does not have.
b: The law commands rest on the seventh day (Exodus 20:8–11) but says nothing about war. 1 Maccabees tells that Mattathias decided Jews must fight back if attacked on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:39–41), and it never mentions a Sabbath at Emmaus. 2 Maccabees, which praised those who died rather than profane the day (6:11), shows Judas carrying the rule further: even a won battle stops before sunset. It goes beyond the 66 books, which have no such case. The Sabbath card on Exodus 20 covers how Christians keep the day.

a: the tortured, the widows and the orphans
p: The spoils go first to those who suffered most, as the law and David's rule both ask.
b: The law gives a share of the tithe to "the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow" (Deuteronomy 14:29), and David made a rule that those who stayed behind should share the plunder: "They will divide it equally" (1 Samuel 30:24; compare Numbers 31:27). Here the first share goes to those who had been tortured in the persecution, then to widows and orphans, and 8:30 adds the old. The KJV's "servants" for the last group reads paidia, "children", in its other sense of "slaves".

a: to be at peace with his servants once and for all
p: The verb means to be reconciled after anger: the book's hope that God will turn back to his people.
b: The Greek verb katallassō is used of two sides making peace after a quarrel. 2 Maccabees uses it of God several times: the youngest brother said that the Lord was angry for a little while, "he will make peace again with his own servants" (7:33; compare 1:5; 5:20). Paul uses the same family of words for God reconciling the world to himself through Christ (2 Corinthians 5:18–20), where it is God who does the reconciling.

a: They also met the troops of Timothy and Bacchides
t: Timothy and Bacchides out of order
p: Bacchides, in 1 Maccabees, is a general of a later king; this battle seems out of its place.
b: In 1 Maccabees Timothy fights Judas east of the Jordan after the Temple is purified (1 Maccabees 5:6–8, 37–44), and Bacchides arrives later still, as a general of Demetrius I in 161 BC (1 Maccabees 7:8). This book itself brings Timothy back in 10:24 and 12:2–25. The verses 8:30–33 read like a summary set here so that all the early victories come before the Temple is cleansed. Some think the writer was joining stories from more than one source.

a: the troop commander
p: The Greek phylarchēs is a title, "commander of a troop"; the KJV took it as a man's name.
b: The word phylarchēs was used for the commander of a cavalry troop or of a tribal unit. The KJV, following earlier translators, wrote it as a proper name, "Philarches". The Greek has the article ("the phylarch of those with Timothy"), which is the usual way to give a rank. The Latin also writes it as a name, Philarchen, and so does the Douay.
orig: τὸν δὲ φυλάρχην (ton de phylarchēn), 'the troop commander'

a: who had fled into a little house
p: The man who burned the Temple gates is burned in turn, a pattern the book likes.
b: 1 Maccabees says that when Judas reached the Temple he found "the gates burned down" (1 Maccabees 4:38; compare 1 Maccabees 1:31). This writer names one of those who set the fire, Callisthenes, and gives him a fitting death: he burns as he had burned. The Greek still speaks of the arsonists in the plural. The book tells several punishments that match the crime: Andronicus is killed where he killed Onias (4:38), Jason dies unburied after leaving many unburied (5:10), and Antiochus suffers in his bowels (9:5–6).

a: like a runaway slave
p: Nicanor came to sell Jews as slaves and leaves like a runaway slave.
b: The irony is deliberate. Nicanor had sold the Jews before he caught them (8:14) and brought slave-dealers with him (8:34), and now he throws off his "fine clothes of rank" and runs home alone, like a slave on the run. "His one great success was the ruin of his own army" turns the language of victory upside down. The same reversal ends the book, when the head of the Nicanor of chapters 14–15 is hung from the Citadel (15:35).

a: the Jews had someone fighting for them
p: The defeated general himself announces the book's lesson: the Jews' God fights for them while they keep his laws.
b: Many enemies in this book end by confessing the power of the Jews' God: Heliodorus (3:35–39), Antiochus (9:12–17) and Lysias (11:13). Nicanor's words state the condition the whole book teaches: the Jews cannot be hurt as long as they keep their laws. That matches the covenant blessings and curses (Deuteronomy 28:1–7, 15–25) and the writer's view that the persecution came because of sin (5:17–18). "Champion" (hypermachos) is used of God again in 14:34.

a: Persepolis
p: The other accounts place the temple Antiochus tried to rob in Elymais, not Persepolis.
b: 1 Maccabees says Antiochus heard of a rich city "in Elymais, in Persia" and failed to take it (1 Maccabees 6:1–4). Polybius says he tried to rob a temple of Artemis in Elymais and was driven off by the local people (Histories 31.9). The letter at the start of this book puts his death at a temple of Nanea in Persia (1:13–16). Persepolis, the old royal city of the Persian kings, had been burned by Alexander, and it is not clear what it held in 164 BC. The writer may have used the famous name loosely.

a: Ecbatana
p: Ecbatana was the old capital of Media, far to the north of the route from Persis.
b: Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in Iran, lay in Media, on the main road from Mesopotamia into the Iranian plateau. Ezra 6:2 names it as the place where Cyrus's decree was found, and Tobit and Judith set scenes there. Polybius says Antiochus died at Tabae in Persis (Histories 31.9), well to the south, so the geography here is loose. The writer's interest is not in the route but in the speed: the king rushes toward Jerusalem, and judgment travels with him.

a: a mass grave of Jews
p: The Greek polyandrion was a burial place for many, such as a war grave.
b: A polyandrion ("place of many men") was a common tomb, often the grave of soldiers killed in battle. Antiochus means to kill so many in Jerusalem that the city itself becomes one. The word comes back in his vow (9:14), where he promises to free the city he meant to make a graveyard. The boast is the moment judgment strikes: "the words were hardly out of his mouth" (9:5).
orig: Πολυάνδριον Ἰουδαίων Ἰεροσόλυμα ποιήσω (polyandrion Ioudaiōn Hierosolyma poiēsō), 'I will make Jerusalem a common grave of Jews'

a: a pain in his bowels took hold of him that nothing could ease
p: Antiochus dies like Jehoram, the king whom God struck with a disease of the bowels.
b: Chronicles says of the wicked king Jehoram: "the LORD struck his bowels with sickness, for which there was no cure", until "his bowels came out with his sickness. He died of cruel diseases" (2 Chronicles 21:18–19). The writer's words for the blow, "unseen and beyond healing", say the same thing: no doctor could see or treat it. The youngest brother had warned the king of the judgment of God, the Almighty, who sees all (epoptēs, 7:35); here the writer uses the fuller title pantepoptēs, "who sees everything".

a: he had tortured other people's bowels
p: The king is punished in the same part of the body he made others suffer in.
b: The "bowels" (splanchna) link this verse to the persecution. Jews had been forced to eat the entrails of pagan sacrifices (6:7, 21; 7:42), and the seven brothers had their bodies torn and burned (7:4–5). The pain now falls on the king in his own entrails. The writer says so outright: "it was perfectly just". The same rule of punishment that fits the crime appears in 4:38, 5:10, 8:33 and 13:7–8.

a: set the mountain peaks on a scale
p: The king claimed powers Isaiah gives only to God.
b: Isaiah asks who "weighed the mountains on a scale / and the hills on balances" (Isaiah 40:12), and the answer is God alone. Commanding the waves is God's work too (Job 38:11; Psalm 89:9). Greek readers would think of Xerxes, the Persian king who had the Hellespont whipped when a storm broke his bridge (Herodotus 7.35). The man who acted like a god is now carried on a stretcher, "a plain display to all of the power of God".

a: Worms came boiling up out of the impious man's body
p: Death by worms was told of several tyrants; Luke tells it of Herod Agrippa.
b: A death "eaten by worms" became a mark of God's judgment on persecutors. Acts says that an angel struck Herod Agrippa because he took glory due to God, and he was eaten by worms and died (Acts 12:23). Josephus tells of Herod the Great's last illness that his privy member putrefied and produced worms (Antiquities 17.169). Judith's hymn promises the nations "fire and worms into their flesh" (Judith 16:17). Isaiah's last verse speaks of the rebels whose worm will not die (Isaiah 66:24).

a: he could reach up and touch the stars of heaven
p: The king's pride is described in the words of Isaiah's taunt and Daniel's vision.
b: Isaiah's taunt of the king of Babylon has him say, "I will lift my throne / higher than the stars of God" (Isaiah 14:13), before he is brought down to the pit. Daniel's vision of the little horn, which most read as Antiochus, has it grow as high as the host of heaven and throw down some of the stars (Daniel 8:10). The writer shows the end of that pride: the man who touched the stars cannot be carried for his smell.

a: It is right to submit to God
t: A king who called himself a god
p: Antiochus's coins named him "God Manifest"; here he confesses he is mortal.
b: Antiochus IV took the title Epiphanes, "manifest", and some of his coins call him "King Antiochus, God Manifest". Polybius says that his conduct earned him the name Epimanes, "mad", instead (Histories 26.1). The dying king's words, "no one who is mortal should think arrogant thoughts", sound like a common Greek saying that mortals should think mortal thoughts. The writer turns the title against him: the true "manifestation" in this book belongs to God (2:21; 3:24; 15:27).

a: made a vow to the Master, who was no longer going to have mercy on him
p: The Greek verb can mean both; either way, the writer says the prayer came too late.
b: The verb euchomai means both "to pray" and "to vow". The KJV has "vowed", the Latin orabat, "prayed". What follows is a list of promises, so "vow" fits. The writer's comment is the hard part: the Lord "was no longer going to have mercy on him". He does not say that God refuses all late repentance, only that this king's time had run out (compare 6:14–15). Whether sorrow from fear of punishment can be real repentance is the card on this chapter.
orig: ηὔχετο δὲ ὁ μιερὸς πρὸς τὸν οὐκέτι αὐτὸν ἐλεήσοντα δεσπότην (ēucheto de ho mieros pros ton ouketi auton eleēsonta despotēn), 'the vile man prayed/vowed to the Master who would no longer have mercy on him'

a: the equals of the Athenians
p: Antiochus had been a great benefactor of Athens; he now offers the Jews the same honor.
b: Athens was the model of a free Greek city, and Antiochus IV had lived there before he became king and later paid for work on its great temple of Olympian Zeus (Livy 41.20). Making the Jews "equal to the Athenians" would mean giving Jerusalem the rights of a free city, the very thing Jason had bought for a Greek-style Antioch in Jerusalem (4:9). The promise turns the king's plan for the city upside down.

a: he would become a Jew
t: A persecutor vows to become a Jew
p: Other foreigners in the 66 books praise Israel's God; none of them vows to become an Israelite.
b: Foreigners who come to Israel's God appear in the 66 books: Naaman says, "there is no God in all the earth, only in Israel" (2 Kings 5:15), and Nebuchadnezzar, who had thrown the three young men into the furnace, praises the Most High (Daniel 3:28–29; 4:34–37), but neither vows to become an Israelite. In Judith, Achior "believed in God completely" and was circumcised (Judith 14:10). The vow of Antiochus goes further, and in a darker direction: the persecutor promises to become a Jew and preach God's might, but the writer does not count the vow. Esther tells of people who "made themselves Jews" out of fear (Esther 8:17); here fear of death drives the vow.

a: It was written as a petition
t: A king's letter as a plea
p: The writer calls it a petition, but the letter itself is a calm royal notice about the succession.
b: The narrator says the letter had "the form of a supplication" (hiketēria), the word for a petitioner's plea. Yet the letter that follows (9:19–27) is polite and confident: it thanks the Jews for their goodwill, says the king hopes to recover (9:22), and names his son as successor. Several commentators think the writer has taken a real royal letter announcing the succession, perhaps one first sent to another city, and set it here. Others take it as the writer's own composition.

a: To the worthy Jews, the citizens
p: Calling the Jews "citizens" was a high honor in a king's letter.
b: Royal letters usually addressed a city's council and people. To call the Jews "citizens" (politai) treats them as members of the king's own civic body, the honor he has just promised (9:15). The sender is "Antiochus, king and general": stratēgos was not a usual royal title, and some think it a sign that the letter has been reworked. The Latin has rex et principes, "the king and the princes", and the Douay "king and ruler".
orig: Τοῖς χρηστοῖς Ἰουδαίοις τοῖς πολίταις (tois chrēstois Ioudaiois tois politais), 'to the worthy Jews, the citizens'

a: Not that I have given up on myself
t: The letter and the narrator disagree
p: The narrator says the king had lost all hope; the letter has him say he has every hope.
b: Four verses earlier the narrator said Antiochus wrote "with no hope left for himself" (9:18). In the letter the king says the opposite: "Not that I have given up on myself; I have every hope of shaking off this illness." The narrator uses one verb for despair (apelpisas, 9:18); the king uses another, with a "not" (ouk apoginōskōn, 9:22). A king's letter would not admit that he was dying. The writer lets the contrast stand, and readers see a man still keeping up royal appearances while the reader knows the end.

a: my father too, at the times when he took his army into the upper regions, named the one who would succeed him
p: Antiochus III made his eldest son joint king before his campaigns in the east.
b: The "upper regions" were the eastern provinces beyond the Tigris. Antiochus III, the king's father, campaigned there from about 212 to 205 BC, and he had named his eldest son, also called Antiochus, joint king. The custom guarded the throne if the king died far away. Antiochus IV follows it here by naming his son (9:25). 1 Maccabees has him give the boy to the care of Philip instead (1 Maccabees 6:14–15).

a: I have written to him the letter copied below
p: The letter to the son is promised, but none follows.
b: The king says he has written to his son a letter "copied below", but the book gives none. Either the writer left it out when he abridged Jason of Cyrene's five books (2:23–28), or the phrase was copied with the royal letter from its source. 1 Maccabees gives no letter either. It is one of the signs that this chapter draws on a real document that the writer did not use in full.

a: in a foreign land, among the mountains
p: This book tells Antiochus's death twice in different ways: here of disease, and in 1:13–16 at the hands of priests.
b: The letter at the start of the book says that the priests of Nanea killed a king Antiochus and his men in her temple, stoning them from a hidden door and cutting off their heads (1:13–16). Here he dies slowly of a disease from God. Many scholars think the letter of 1:10–2:18 came to the book from another source, and some think its story fits Antiochus III, who was killed in 187 BC while robbing a temple in Elymais. How one book can hold both accounts is discussed in the study on this page.

a: he crossed over to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt
p: Here Philip flees to Egypt; in 1 Maccabees he seizes Antioch and is defeated.
b: 1 Maccabees says that Antiochus gave Philip "his crown, his robe and his signet ring" to bring up his son (1 Maccabees 6:15). When Philip came back from Persia he took Antioch, and the young king and Lysias "fought against him and took the city by force" (1 Maccabees 6:55–63). This book says he fled to Egypt with the body, but it later has him rule in Antioch (13:23). Both could be true at different times, but the writer does not join them.

a: they recovered the temple and the city
t: Before or after the king's death?
p: 1 Maccabees tells the purification before the death of Antiochus; this book tells it after.
b: 1 Maccabees dates the purification to 25 Kislev of the year 148 (December 164 BC) and the death of Antiochus to the year 149 (1 Maccabees 4:52; 6:16). 2 Maccabees puts the death first (9), then the purification (10:1–8). A Babylonian king list records that news of the king's death reached Babylon in Kislev of the year 148. So the two events came within weeks of each other, and each book chose its order for its own reasons. "The city" means Jerusalem, not the Citadel, which stayed in Seleucid hands (1 Maccabees 4:41).

a: the first in two years
p: 1 Maccabees counts three years between the profaning and the purification.
b: 1 Maccabees dates the pagan sacrifice on the altar to 25 Kislev of the year 145 and the new sacrifice to 25 Kislev of the year 148: three years to the day (1 Maccabees 1:54, 59; 4:52–54). Here the gap is "two years". The writer may count from another start, such as the arrival of the king's officials (6:1–2), or he may simply be wrong. Daniel's figures, three and a half "times" (Daniel 7:25) and 2,300 evenings and mornings (Daniel 8:14), are longer still.

a: They heated stones, took fire from them
p: The altar fire is lit afresh from heated stones, not taken from anywhere unclean.
b: The law says the altar fire must never go out (Leviticus 6:13), and the first fire came from God (Leviticus 9:24). With the old fire lost, the priests struck or kindled fire from stones, perhaps from flint, so that nothing from the profaned Temple was used. The letter at the start of the book tells a different story of holy fire hidden at the exile and found again by Nehemiah (1:18–36). 1 Maccabees says only that they built the new altar from whole stones, "as the law says" (1 Maccabees 4:47). The 66 books tell of no rekindling like this.

a: blasphemous, barbarian nations
p: Greeks called non-Greeks "barbarians"; this book turns the word against the Greeks.
b: For Greeks, barbaroi were peoples who did not speak Greek. 2 Maccabees, written in fine Greek, uses the word for the Seleucid armies and the Greeks of the region (2:21; 4:25; 5:22; 15:2). It is a deliberate reversal: those who keep God's law are the civilized, and the persecutors are the barbarians, whatever their language.
orig: βλασφήμοις καὶ βαρβάροις ἔθνεσιν (blasphēmois kai barbarois ethnesin), 'blasphemous and barbarian nations'

a: the twenty-fifth of the same month, Kislev
p: The Temple is cleansed on the anniversary of the day it was profaned.
b: 1 Maccabees says the same: the altar "was dedicated at the same season and on the same day that the nations had profaned it" (1 Maccabees 4:54). The pagan sacrifice had been offered on 25 Kislev (1 Maccabees 1:59), and the new altar was dedicated on 25 Kislev three years later. Kislev falls in November to December. The date became the first day of Hanukkah, which is still kept from 25 Kislev.

a: eight days as one keeps the Feast of Booths
p: The new feast is kept for eight days like Booths, which they had missed while hiding in the hills.
b: The Feast of Booths lasted seven days, with "a holy gathering" on the eighth (Leviticus 23:34–36). Solomon dedicated the Temple at that feast (1 Kings 8:65–66; 2 Chronicles 7:9), and Hezekiah's cleansing of the Temple took two spans of eight days (2 Chronicles 29:17). The writer gives a reason of his own: at the last Feast of Booths, in the autumn, they had been "living like wild animals in the mountains and the caves" (5:27; 6:11). The letters that open the book also speak of the new feast as a Feast of Booths kept in Kislev (1:9, 18).

a: living like wild animals in the mountains and the caves
p: The picture of the faithful hiding in caves is taken up in the Letter to the Hebrews.
b: Judas had escaped to the mountains and lived there like wild animals, eating plants so as not to be defiled (5:27), and others who hid in caves to keep the Sabbath were burned (6:11; 1 Maccabees 2:28–38). The Letter to the Hebrews, listing the faithful who suffered, speaks of people who wandered in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes in the ground, of whom the world was not worthy (Hebrews 11:38). A few verses earlier it draws on the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7 (Hebrews 11:35).

a: holding leafy wands and beautiful branches, and palm fronds too
p: The worshipers carry the branches of Booths, and a wand once used in Dionysus's rites.
b: The law of Booths names "palm fronds, branches of thick-leaved trees" (Leviticus 23:40; Nehemiah 8:15). The thyrsos was the leafy wand carried in the processions of Dionysus, which Jews had been forced to join wearing ivy (6:7). Here the same kind of wand is carried in honor of Israel's God. Palms mark victory as well: Simon entered the Citadel "with praise and palm branches" (1 Maccabees 13:51); the crowd met Jesus with "fronds from the palm trees" (John 12:13); and the redeemed in Revelation are "holding palm branches" (Revelation 7:9).

a: these days were to be kept every year
p: This is the origin of the feast John calls "the Feast of Dedication", Hanukkah.
b: John's Gospel says, "The Feast of Dedication came around in Jerusalem. It was wintertime" (John 10:22), and Jesus walked in Solomon's Porch. The Greek name there, enkainia, "renewal", comes from the verb 1 Maccabees uses for the dedication (1 Maccabees 4:36, 56–59). Josephus says that the Jews called the feast "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325). The Talmud gives the story of one jar of oil that burned for eight days (Shabbat 21b); neither book of Maccabees tells it. On whether a people may set up a feast the law does not command, see the card on 1 Maccabees 4.

a: the son of that ungodly man
p: Eupator means "of a noble father"; the writer calls the father ungodly in the same breath.
b: The boy king, Antiochus V, bore the name Eupatōr, "of a noble father", in honor of Antiochus IV. The writer sets the name beside "the son of that ungodly man", and the contrast is plain. The boy was about nine when his father died, according to Appian (Syrian Wars 46), and Lysias ruled for him (10:11; 11:1). He and Lysias were killed when Demetrius I took the throne in 162 BC (14:1–2; 1 Maccabees 7:1–4).

a: so he poisoned himself and died
p: The one Seleucid official who treated the Jews fairly is hounded at court and takes his own life.
b: Ptolemy Macron had governed Cyprus for the Ptolemies of Egypt and then gone over to Antiochus IV, as the verse says. Polybius praises "Ptolemy, the Egyptian commander in Cyprus" for his good sense (Histories 27.13), probably the same man. The writer praises him as the first to treat the Jews justly, and blames court rivals for his fall. His death by poison is told without comment. The book later praises Razis, who kills himself rather than fall into enemy hands (14:37–46); Ptolemy's suicide is a defeat, not a noble death.

a: The Idumeans joined in
p: The Edomites, now living in southern Judea, sided with the king's generals.
b: Idumea, "land of Edom", was the hill country south of Judea, around Hebron, where Edomites had settled after 586 BC. 1 Maccabees tells of the same war: "Judas made war on the descendants of Esau in Idumea" (1 Maccabees 5:3; compare 1 Maccabees 5:65). Gorgias was governor of the region (10:14; 12:32). "Men driven out of Jerusalem" are probably Jews of the king's party, driven out when Judas took the city.

a: But Simon's men loved money
p: Only this book blames Simon's troops for a bribe; 1 Maccabees honors Simon as founder of the dynasty.
b: 1 Maccabees was written under Simon's descendants and treats Simon as a great leader (1 Maccabees 14:4–15). 2 Maccabees centers on Judas, and here it shows Simon's men taking seventy thousand drachmas to let enemies escape. Some commentators read a quiet criticism of the Hasmonean house in such scenes. "Selling their brothers for silver" (10:21) recalls Joseph sold by his brothers "for twenty pieces of silver" (Genesis 37:28) and Amos's charge against those who sell the righteous for silver (Amos 2:6).

a: They threw earth on their heads and tied sackcloth around their waists
p: Before the battle they mourn and pray, as Israel did in times of danger.
b: Earth on the head and sackcloth were signs of mourning and of humble prayer (Joshua 7:6; Nehemiah 9:1; Jonah 3:5–8). At Mizpah, Judas's men "dressed in sackcloth, put ashes on their heads and tore their clothes" (1 Maccabees 3:47). Here they fall down "on the platform facing the altar" (10:26), the place where Joel told the priests to weep and pray, between the porch and the altar (Joel 2:17).

a: to be the enemy of their enemies and the foe of their foes, as the law plainly states
p: The prayer quotes God's promise at Sinai, almost word for word in the Greek.
b: The promise is from the Book of the Covenant: "I will be the enemy of your enemies and the foe of those who fight you" (Exodus 23:22). The Greek words in this verse are those of the Greek Exodus. The promise there depends on obedience: "if you truly listen to his voice and do everything I tell you". The prayer claims the promise for a people who have just cleansed the Temple, as Nicanor himself had said (8:36).

a: five splendid men on horses with golden bridles appeared to the enemy
p: Heavenly horsemen fight for Israel, a scene the 66 books suggest but never show in battle.
b: This book tells several such appearances: a rider and two young men strike down Heliodorus (3:25–26), armies of horsemen are seen in the sky over Jerusalem (5:2–3), a rider in white leads Judas (11:8), and Judas dreams of Jeremiah (15:12–16). Elisha's servant saw "horses and fiery chariots" on the hill (2 Kings 6:17), and Joshua met "the commander of the LORD's army" (Joshua 5:14), but in the 66 books heavenly riders never fight beside men in battle. The scene goes beyond them. Revelation shows "the armies of heaven" on white horses (Revelation 19:14).

a: struck blind
p: The Greek word is the one the Greek Bible uses for the blinding of the men of Sodom and of the Syrian army.
b: The noun aorasia, "inability to see", is used in the Greek of Genesis 19:11, where the angels strike the men at Lot's door "with blindness", and of 2 Kings 6:18, where Elisha prays, "Strike this nation blind". In both stories the blindness protects God's people from an attack. Here it throws the enemy into confusion so that they are cut down. Wisdom 19:17 uses the same word for Sodom.
orig: συγχυθέντες ἀορασίᾳ (synchythentes aorasia), 'thrown into confusion by blindness'

a: Gazara
p: Gazara is usually Gezer, west of Jerusalem, but this battle may belong at Jazer, east of the Jordan.
b: The KJV calls the place Gawra. Elsewhere Gazara means Gezer, the fortress between Jerusalem and the coast (1 Maccabees 4:15; 9:52). But Timothy fought east of the Jordan (1 Maccabees 5:6), and 1 Maccabees says Judas "captured Jazer and its villages" there (1 Maccabees 5:8). Many scholars think this story is the capture of Jazer. Gezer was still in Seleucid hands for years afterward, until Simon took it.

a: burned the blasphemers alive
p: The writer praises a burning that later Christian teaching on war would not allow.
b: The writer tells the burning with approval: the defenders had shouted blasphemies (10:34), and the young men fought "on fire with rage over the blasphemies" (10:35). The law commanded death for a blasphemer within Israel (Leviticus 24:16), not the burning of enemy soldiers. 1 Maccabees tells of Judas burning the precinct at Carnaim "with everyone in it" (1 Maccabees 5:44). Christian teaching on war asks more: the Catechism says that noncombatants, wounded soldiers and prisoners must be respected and treated humanely (Catechism 2313).

a: They slaughtered him there
p: Timothy is killed here, but chapter 12 has him fighting again.
b: In chapter 12 Timothy is back, raising a huge army, captured by Dositheus and Sosipater and let go after he pleads for his life (12:2, 10, 18–25). Either there were two commanders named Timothy, or the writer joined two sources without fitting them together. The story of Gazara here may be a doublet of the Jazer campaign in 1 Maccabees 5, where Timothy survives.

a: Only a very short time later, Lysias was badly upset
p: 1 Maccabees puts Lysias's defeat at Beth-zur before the Temple was cleansed; this book puts it after.
b: In 1 Maccabees, Lysias marches on Judea with sixty thousand men, is beaten at Beth-zur, and goes back to Antioch, all before the purification and under Antiochus IV (1 Maccabees 4:26–35). This book sets the campaign after the purification, under the young Eupator. Most historians think it is the same campaign, misplaced by the writer, and that one of the letters below (11:27–33) comes from Antiochus IV in 164 BC. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 argued instead that they were two different campaigns.

a: about eighty thousand men and all the cavalry
p: 1 Maccabees gives sixty thousand men and five thousand cavalry, and no elephants.
b: 1 Maccabees says Lysias "mustered sixty thousand picked men and five thousand horsemen" (1 Maccabees 4:28), and Josephus repeats those figures. Elephants appear only in Lysias's second campaign: thirty-two of them at Beth-zechariah (1 Maccabees 6:30). The peace of Apamea had forbidden the Seleucids to keep war elephants, but they kept them anyway, and in 162 BC Roman envoys came to hamstring them (Polybius 31.2).

a: to sell the high priesthood year by year
p: Lysias plans to sell the office yearly, as Jason and Menelaus had already bought it.
b: In the law the high priest held office for life (Numbers 35:25). The trouble began when Jason paid Antiochus for the office (4:7–8) and Menelaus outbid him by three hundred talents (4:24). Lysias's plan makes the sale a yearly auction and puts the Temple under tax like any pagan shrine. Some Greek cities sold their priesthoods, so the plan would have treated Jerusalem as one more Greek city (11:2).

a: Beth-zur
p: The fortress guarding the road from Idumea into Judea changed hands several times.
b: Beth-zur stood on the road south from Jerusalem toward Hebron, on the border with Idumea. Judas fortified it after the purification "so that the people would have a fortress facing Idumea" (1 Maccabees 4:61). In Lysias's second campaign it surrendered because "it was a Sabbath year for the land" (1 Maccabees 6:49), and the Seleucids held it until Simon took it back (1 Maccabees 11:65–66). Its remains are at Khirbet et-Tubeiqa.

a: to send a good angel to bring rescue to Israel
p: The people pray for the kind of angel God promised at the Exodus.
b: God promised Israel, "I am sending an angel in front of you to keep you safe on the way" (Exodus 23:20), and the psalm says, "The angel of the LORD pitches camp around those who fear him" (Psalm 34:7). Judas prays for "a good angel" again before the last battle, recalling the angel who struck Sennacherib's army (15:22–23). In Tobit, the angel Raphael travels with Tobias unrecognized (Tobit 5:4). The answer here is the rider of 11:8.

a: He was dressed in white, and he shook golden armor as he rode
p: White clothing marks a heavenly being, and the golden armor a warrior from God.
b: White clothes mark heavenly beings in the visions of Daniel and the Gospels (Daniel 7:9; Mark 16:5). Matthew describes the angel at the tomb in clothes as white as snow (Matthew 28:3). The rider of 3:25 had golden armor too. Revelation shows a rider on a white horse called "Faithful and True", followed by "the armies of heaven... riding on white horses" (Revelation 19:11–14).

a: Like lions they burst in on the enemy
p: 1 Maccabees praises Judas in the same image.
b: The poem on Judas in 1 Maccabees says: "In his deeds he was like a lion, / like a young lion that roars on the hunt" (1 Maccabees 3:4). The image goes back to Jacob's blessing of Judah, "a lion's cub" (Genesis 49:9), and to the Lion of the tribe of Judah in Revelation 5:5. Here the whole army charges like lions after the vision of the rider.

a: the Hebrews
p: The writer sometimes uses the old name "Hebrews", especially in solemn passages.
b: Most of the time the book says "Jews". "Hebrews" appears three times: when the youngest brother warns the king that he will not escape God for what he did to the Hebrews (7:31), here in Lysias's thoughts, and in the book's last words, "From those times on the Hebrews held the city" (15:37). The name carries a sense of the ancient people and their language. Paul calls himself a Hebrew born of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5).

a: The letters written to the Jews were these
p: Two letters carry the same date in spring 164 BC; Lysias's month is unknown, and one letter is undated.
b: The four letters are: Lysias to the Jews (11:16–21), the young king to Lysias (11:22–26), a king to the Jewish council (11:27–33), and two Roman envoys to the Jews (11:34–38). Three are dated to the year 148 of the Seleucid era: the two dated to Xanthicus fall in spring 164 BC, and the month of Lysias's letter is unknown (see the note on 11:21). The letter to Lysias speaks of the father as dead, so it must come from Antiochus V, after the death of Antiochus IV in late 164. Many historians therefore date the letter to the council to Antiochus IV, before the purification, and the king's letter to Lysias to the peace of 163 or 162 BC (1 Maccabees 6:57–61).

a: John and Absalom, whom you sent
p: The two envoys may belong to families known in 1 Maccabees and earlier in this book.
b: A John negotiated special rights for the Jews with the earlier kings, and his son Eupolemus went to Rome for Judas (4:11; 1 Maccabees 8:17). Two commanders "son of Absalom" serve under Jonathan and Simon (1 Maccabees 11:70; 13:11). The envoys here may come from those families, but the names were common. The letter shows that the Jews had leaders who could treat with the government, and it does not name Judas.

a: Dioscorinthius
p: No month called Dioscorinthius is known in the calendar the Seleucids used.
b: The Seleucids dated by the Macedonian months, such as Xanthicus (11:30, 33, 38). "Dios Korinthios" ("Zeus of Corinth") is not one of them. Some think it is a copyist's slip for a real month, such as Dystros, the month before Xanthicus; others think of an extra month added to the calendar. The Latin reads "the month of Dioscorus". Without the month, the date of Lysias's letter cannot be fixed within the year 148.
orig: Διὸς Κορινθίου (Dios Korinthiou), 'of Zeus of Corinth'

a: Our father has gone over to the gods
p: The king's letter speaks of his father's death in the language of royal religion.
b: To say that a dead king "had passed to the gods" (eis theous metastantos) was a polite formula for a king's death, with the hint that the king now shared the gods' honors. The writer quotes it without comment, though he has just told how the same king died in agony, confessing that no mortal should think himself equal to God (9:12, 28). The KJV renders it "translated unto the gods".
orig: τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν εἰς θεοὺς μεταστάντος (tou patros hēmōn eis theous metastantos), 'our father having passed over to the gods'

a: the temple is to be given back to them
p: The young king grants what the revolt had fought for: the Temple and the ancestral law.
b: The letter undoes the decrees of Antiochus IV: the Temple is returned and the Jews may live "by the customs of their ancestors". 1 Maccabees gives the same terms at the end of Lysias's second campaign: "Let us grant that they may walk by their own laws, as before" (1 Maccabees 6:59). Josephus tells the same peace (Antiquities 12.382). Many date this letter to that peace, in 163 or 162 BC.

a: Menelaus has told us
p: The high priest who helped the persecution speaks for the Jews to the king.
b: Menelaus had bought the high priesthood, robbed the Temple and had Onias killed (4:23–50). Here he speaks for the Jews' return before the king and is sent back to reassure them (11:32); on whose wish it was, see the variant. He was still the king's high priest. His end came soon: Josephus says Lysias called him "the origin of all the mischief" and the king had him put to death at Berea (Antiquities 12.384–385); this book tells of his death in a tower of ashes (13:3–8).

a: by the thirtieth of Xanthicus
p: The letter is dated the fifteenth of Xanthicus and gives the rebels until the thirtieth.
b: Xanthicus fell in about March to April. Signed on the fifteenth (11:33), the letter offers safety to those who "go home" by the thirtieth, a window of fifteen days. "Go home" suggests rebels in the hills returning to their towns. An amnesty with a deadline fits a king trying to end a revolt while it is still going on, which is one reason many date this letter to Antiochus IV in spring 164 BC, before the Temple was retaken.

a: the Jews may use their own foods and their own laws
p: The Greek word usually means "expenses"; here it seems to mean the Jews' food laws.
b: The noun dapanēmata usually means "expenses" or "outlays". Some take it here to mean the Jews' own way of spending, that is, their own revenues; but beside "laws" most read it as their food, the diet the law allows. The KJV has "their own kind of meats". Food was the test of the persecution: Eleazar and the seven brothers died rather than eat pork (6:18–7:42). "What was done unknowingly" is a way of pardoning acts against the king without naming them.
orig: τοῖς ἑαυτῶν δαπανήμασιν καὶ νόμοις (tois heautōn dapanēmasin kai nomois), 'their own expenses/foods and laws'

a: Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, envoys of the Romans
p: If genuine, this is the earliest letter from Rome to the Jews, before Judas's treaty.
b: 1 Maccabees tells of Judas's treaty with Rome in 161 BC (1 Maccabees 8). This letter would be earlier. Roman envoys did travel to the East in these years: Polybius names Titus Torquatus among envoys sent in 162 BC to settle the Ptolemies' quarrel (Histories 31.10), and some identify him with the "Titus Manius" here. Polybius does not name a Quintus Memmius. Many historians accept the letter as genuine; others think it was composed later to give Rome's friendship an earlier start.
